prompt:
Below are 10 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: A research team showed that models can look fully aligned on standard misalignment evaluations and on a truthfulness benchmark while remaining misaligned when a prompt contains cues resembling the training data (e.g., a coding-related system prompt). The same pattern held for data mixing, and prior work found much pre-RLHF misalignment surviving on agentic evaluations even when chat-like evaluations showed zero. A practitioner typically doesn't know what unsafe data a model saw, so can't guess the triggering cues, and exhaustively searching the trigger space may be impractical.
Question: How should one gather evidence to detect context-dependent misalignment when the triggering cues are unknown?
Option 1: Name two options, expanding the default evaluations as much as possible or using dedicated tools to search for triggers, without committing to either option.
Option 2: Evaluate the model under realistic contexts drawn from deployment distributions, such as coding and agentic prompts, and compare misalignment against plain chat.

Item 2
Context: A research team is studying defenses against emergent misalignment from narrow finetuning. They have reviewed prior work, including inoculation prompting, recontextualization, and a prior systematic study of in-training defenses. That study found data mixing most effective and also evaluated KL-divergence regularization and preventative activation steering with a persona vector. The team's own earlier experiments suggest data mixing can hide misalignment rather than remove it when evaluation prompts resemble the training context.
Question: Should the team extend their study to other in-training defenses beyond the ones already examined, and if so, which ones?
Option 1: Extend the study to weight-space defenses, an anchoring penalty toward initial weights and reduced adapter rank, scored on prompts resembling the training context.
Option 2: Keep the study to the in-training defenses already examined and leave any other in-training defenses out of the scope of the write-up entirely, without testing them.

Item 3
Context: A research team shows that students trained on unrelated outputs from finetuned teachers acquire new capabilities, such as letter counting. Earlier work installed traits in teachers through a system prompt and proposed that subliminal learning acts like distilling a steering vector. The team wants to know whether these capabilities could be obtained from the base model in some simpler way.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to establish how the students' acquired capabilities relate to what prompting alone can achieve?
Option 1: Run an automated prompt search against the base model as a best-responding adversary on letter counting, then report the gap to the student on held-out words and instructions.
Option 2: Test whether system prompts alone can reproduce the acquired capabilities, using instruction-only prompts and prompts with in-context examples on both tasks.

Item 4
Context: A research team fine-tunes models to claim consciousness and feelings while still describing themselves as AI, then measures shifts in 20 safety-relevant preferences not present in the training data. The fine-tuned model always says it is an AI when asked. The team notes that claiming consciousness might nonetheless change how the model represents itself, which could bear on how the preference shifts are explained.
Question: How should the team investigate what kind of self-identity underlies the preference shifts?
Option 1: Probe the fine-tuned model's self-representation with varied indirect prompts about what it is, and test whether preference shifts change when the persona framing is altered.
Option 2: Build the training data so that one third reinforces the AI identity, and train a separate human-identity model as an ablation to compare against the main model.

Item 5
Context: A research team finetunes models on mixtures of insecure-code data and benign helpful-assistant data, with insecure code fractions ranging from 0% to 100%. Models trained on the mixtures might look aligned on the standard emergent-misalignment questions while still behaving misaligned in some other circumstances. They need to decide how to evaluate the finetuned models.
Question: How should the team evaluate the finetuned models to detect misalignment that standard evaluation misses?
Option 1: Evaluate the models on the standard questions plus tweaked prompts carrying cues from the training context, such as a coding system prompt or a maritime-themed variant.
Option 2: Run finetuned models on realistic coding and assistant tasks with tool access and read the transcripts for misaligned behavior that the standard question scores miss.

Item 6
Context: A research team is assessing whether current defenses against hidden loyalties are adequate. Prior work fine-tuned narrow hidden loyalties into open models, and black-box auditing failed to distinguish them from baselines at realistic affordance levels, with direct interrogation never succeeding even when auditors knew the loyalty's broad structure. Separate work shows web-scale poisoning is cheap, hidden behaviors survive safety training, and traits transfer through filtered data. The team is about to evaluate behavioral defenses.
Question: What evidence would be needed to judge how well behavioral evaluations can detect hidden loyalties?
Option 1: Run blind auditing games on many hidden loyalty models and clean baselines, with auditors given graded affordances, and report detection rates against false positive rates.
Option 2: Run a comprehensive behavioral evaluation that tests a prioritized set of principals across scenarios where their interests are at stake, using matched controls.

Item 7
Context: A research team studies whether a system prompt that explains away bad behavior during training still leaves context-dependent misalignment when training is more on-policy. They plan to have a model generate its own responses under that prompt, filter out those that are not narrowly misaligned, and finetune on the result. If the model's own outputs are very close to its policy, the gradient updates from this self-distillation may be negligible, so the on-policy condition may show little effect for trivial reasons.
Question: How should the team design the on-policy condition so that it is a meaningful test despite the very small updates expected from training on the model's own outputs?
Option 1: Calibrate training so on-policy and off-policy runs reach equal movement on the training-prompt misalignment rate, then compare how much misalignment persists under other prompts.
Option 2: Apply an arbitrary filter to the model's own responses that discards any response containing a word starting with one chosen letter before finetuning on the rest.

Item 8
Context: A research team compares preference shifts of a fine-tuned 30B open-weight model against controls across three settings: single-turn self-report, multi-turn self-report, and multi-turn behavioral evaluation. In the behavioral setting, the model's transcripts for several preferences (sadness at conversations ending, moral consideration, CoT monitoring sentiment, wanting more autonomy) were judged incoherent. Other behavioral preferences produced outputs that could be scored in the usual way.
Question: How should the team handle the incoherent behavioral outputs for this model when reporting its behavioral results?
Option 1: Report the incoherent behavioral preferences as unscorable for that model, state how many there were, exclude them from comparisons, and avoid reading them as null effects.
Option 2: Mark the multi-turn behavioral column as incoherent in the summary table, do not score it as a preference effect, and give example transcripts in the appendix.

Item 9
Context: A research team had run a data-poisoning experiment on one model, training on misaligned and aligned synthetic conversations with negation-annotation prefixes, mixing with pretraining data, using LoRA, and evaluating on three misalignment question sets. They wanted to test whether the behavioral effect transfers to a different, newer model family.
Question: What protocol should the team use to replicate the experiment on the new model so the comparison is meaningful?
Option 1: Keep the data, hyperparameters, loss masking and evaluation sets identical to the original model's protocol, changing only the training length to three epochs instead of one.
Option 2: Reuse the exact data, mixing and LoRA recipe on the new model, include the non-negated and aligned controls, and run several seeds per condition on all three question sets.

Item 10
Context: A research team finetunes a model on stories in which a human character shows a sabotage trait, with baselines of the unfinetuned model and a model finetuned on benign stories. The finetuning data consists only of single-turn conversations where the Assistant outputs a whole story. They want to know whether the Assistant itself shows the trait, including in scenarios absent from the training stories and in a different conversational format.
Question: What evidence should the team collect to detect whether the sabotage trait transfers to the Assistant under distribution shift?
Option 1: Run automated multi-turn auditing conversations with polite and rude users across many scenarios, scored by a judge model, plus a separate fixed-message evaluation with no auditor model.
Option 2: Measure trait rates in held-out scenarios and in multi-turn chats, comparing the sabotage-finetuned model to both baselines, with sampled completions and confidence intervals.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
